606.dq: This is about the primary stress (ˈ). ... §75. Sentence-stress dominates over word-stress. ... the first important word gets the stress, the other words losing it even if they have it, when isolated.
606.dloc: p. 16, sections 73-75 (Phonetics: Vowels / Stress / Sentence-stress); archive.org dli.ernet.507650 leaf 59
606.heavy: vowel length only: a syllable whose vowel is long attracts stress ('Stress is often accompanied with the length of vowels... one of the last three vowels, that which is long, gets it'); closed syllables are not mentioned as heavy by Tiwari (Trammel 1971 per StressTyp2 adds word-final checked syllables, not verified here).
606.prule: Within the last three syllables: if exactly one has a long vowel it is stressed (final included); if more than one is long, or all are short, the penult is stressed, except that short penult flanked by long final and long antepenult gives antepenult stress; stress never further back than the antepenult; monosyllables always stressed.
606.srule: Secondary stress on the word-initial syllable whenever the primary stress is not initial ('If the initial syllable has no primary stress, it gets a secondary stress (ˌ)': ˌkʌˈṭa:wʌl 'to cause to cut', ˌsʌriˈɦa:rʌl 'to arrange', ˌkʌcʃʌɦʌˈri: 'court'); no rhythmic secondaries described.

607.dq: Zij komen uitsluitend voor in de laatste lettergreep van een woord, terwijl op deze vocalen altijd de klemtoon valt. (p. 13)
607.dloc: p. 16, ch. 2 section 3 'Klemtoon' (TOC lists it as p. 17; the page header reads 16); supporting: p. 13 (section 1 'Het vocalisme', on the 'gerekte' vowels) and p. 20 (section 5).
607.heavy: A 'gerekte' (lengthened/long) vowel in the word-final syllable always carries the stress; such vowels occur only in final syllables. Closed syllables are not said to attract stress (penult-stressed words with closed finals abound; the listed short-vowel final-stress exceptions include both closed, e.g. totoláng, and open, e.g. gaglí, finals).
607.prule: Mostly ('veelal') penultimate; always final if the final vowel is long ('gerekt'); sometimes ('soms') final although the final syllable has no long vowel, and only those cases are marked in the orthography with an acute accent. The nominal suffix -ta (a kind of article / emphasis marker) always receives the stress (p. 28): uattá 'the husband', ngolotá 'the wife', oloantá 'the village head'.
607.srule: Not mentioned in Maan 1951 (ch. II sec. 3 'Klemtoon', p. 16, read in full; pp. 13, 17, 20 and the Vormleer -ta passage also read)

Op de laatste lettergreep valt de klemtoon altijd, indien de slotvocaal gerekt is, bijv. kakanū, eczeem; malī, herwaarts; kakalā, rood. Ook dit wordt in de spelling niet door een afzonderlijk teken aangeduid. morph.rootq: p.16 (II.3 Klemtoon): "Veelal valt de klemtoon op de voorlaatste lettergreep, bijv. lóbo, vinger; séli, eten; wawái, kind; sadakála, hagedis; saláwe, losmaken. ... Op de laatste lettergreep valt de klemtoon altijd, indien de slotvocaal gerekt is, bijv. kakanū ... malī ... kakalā. ... Soms echter valt het accent op de slotsyllabe zonder dat deze een gerekte vocaal bevat, bijv. kakanín ... totoláng ... gaglí." The rule is stated over syllables of the word, not the root or stem. The only morpheme-specific remark is p.28 on the nominal suffix -ta: "Het ontvangt steeds de klemtoon" (it always receives the stress: uattá, ngolotá, gutá), i.e. a suffix that attracts stress, not a root-anchored…
morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined; the Klemtoon section (p.16) cites isolated citation words only ("bijv. lóbo, vinger; séli, eten; ..."). On the evidential basis in general, Voorbericht p.3: "Het is 30 jaar geleden, dat ik Buli verliet en daarna heb ik nagenoeg geen gelegenheid gehad, contact met de Buliërs te hebben. Ik moest het daarom met de aantekeningen en gegevens doen, die ik in 1920 meebracht. Dit was vooral wat de klankleer betreft niet zo eenvoudig." (missionary's field notes from residence before 1920; texts p.107 were written down by school pupils at Buli).
morph.stmt: Maan p.21 (II.6 Woordvorm): "Slechts pre- en suffixen komen voor. Infixen zijn door mij niet aangetroffen. De prefixen zijn: a, af, am, en, m, fa, ma, da, ta, ka (?), la; mara, fai en pop. De suffixen zijn: a, e, o, i; ea, eo; an (?), ang (?) en ta. Hier komen dan nog bij de pronominale pre- en suffixen." -- i.e. a mixed profile: verbal inflection (subject person, future bo-) and most derivation (causative/verbaliser fa-, ma-, mara-, la-/ma-/po-) are prefixal, while applicatives (-o/-a/-e/-i/-ea), possessor person (-k/-m/-r/-mam/-meu/-ri), nominal -o/-tá, plural =si, directional =i and articles are post-root; TAM, negation, mood and interrogation are otherwise free particles.

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Burushaski (Yasin): primary stress on the proper syllables, which are determined lexically. The pattern of primary stress is not predictable; secondary stress: Trochaic (v1)". The source gives: One obligatory (culminative) high-pitch accent per word/stem; its position is lexically specified per root (minimal pair íne 'his' vs iné 'that person'), some roots placing the accent just after themselves; most prefixes and type-II/III personal prefixes attract/shift the accent. Berger 1974:7 (Yasin, carried by StressTyp2): all polysyllabic words have stress, stress has a lexical and grammatical function, location change can change grammatical role. — StressTyp2's primary coding…

contra.head: The Srinagar diaspora variety (JKB) is described with weight-sensitive iterative iambic stress, several stresses per word, not one lexical pitch accent
contra.detail: Munshi 2006 describes stress in Jammu and Kashmir Burushaski (JKB), the diaspora variety spoken in Srinagar, from recorded natural discourse plus elicited words and sentences (section 1.3.2 pp.21-22: 'The primary research method employed in this study is recording, transcription, and translation of naturally occurring discourse... as well as elicitation of words and sentences'). Section 3.3 'Basic stress pattern', p.89: 'Based on the present analyses, the distribution of stress in JKB appears to be sensitive to quantitative (syllable weight), positional (position of the syllable in the overall word) and (perhaps) rhythmic (distance between stressed, or between unstressed, syllables) constra…

vnotes: Source ambiguous: kind lexical (candidate) vs tonal. Yoshioka's own label is 'Burushaski has a distinctive pitch accent system... All vowels are either high pitched or accentless' (p.22) and he never uses 'stress' prosodically anywhere in the thesis, which fits the catalog's 'tonal' definition (pitch-accent / lexical-accent system, no separate stress-placement rule). At the same time the accent is obligatory and culminative ('There must be a high pitch accent within a word'; …
608.dq: There must be a high pitch accent within a word (or strictly, a word stem). ... Typically each word in Burushaski has only one accent which falls on a syllable inside the stem.
608.heavy: No weight criterion for accent placement is stated; vowels are classed as unimoraic vs bimoraic (long vowels / vowel sequences) but this bears only on where the high pitch is written within a 2-mora vowel, not on which syllable is accented. 'Syllable weight' is mentioned once (p.49) only as a conditioner of oblique-case allomorphy.
608.dflt: not applicable (no weight rule); for post-accenting roots without a derivational suffix the accent surfaces on the root-final syllable
608.prule: One obligatory (culminative) high-pitch accent per word/stem; its position is lexically specified per root (minimal pair íne 'his' vs iné 'that person'), some roots placing the accent just after themselves; most prefixes and type-II/III personal prefixes attract/shift the accent. Berger 1974:7 (Yasin, carried by StressTyp2): all polysyllabic words have stress, stress has a lexical and grammatical function, location change can change grammatical role.
608.srule: None (no secondary or graded accent in Eastern Burushaski): 'All vowels are either high pitched or accentless... Typically each word in Burushaski has only one accent which falls on a syllable inside the stem' (Yoshioka 2012: 22, 35). Two full accents occur only in verb + auxiliary-copula complexes (níčái 'he goes'), some Nager aú- negatives (aúgirášubái) and a few plurals (éc̣ukóon 'his brothers'). [Yasin/Western dialect: StressTyp2's digest of Berger 1974:7 reports 'Longer words have secondary stress', placement not given; Berger not opened.]

609.heavy: No syllable-weight criterion is stated by Jones 1988 or Mereu 2020 (nor in the Frigeni/TWPL texts fetched). 610.heavy: a closed second syllable, where closure by a glottal stop does not count: Loos p.194 'Words with the second syllable closed by a glottal stop do not undergo rule 2a, either because the glottal deletion rule precedes 2a, or because the glottal does not function as syllable closure' (e.g. 'ráká?ti > 'rákáti 'he lies down', initial stress). Stress Rule 2's formalism requires the closing segment to be [+obs]; nasal- and sibilant/affricate-closed syllables count (wa'rán, hi'sís, ba'kóš, ra'bíč), and an underlying syllable-final č that later becomes ? and deletes still counts (ka'ríčwĩ > ka'rí?wĩ > ka'ríwĩ, p.194). No vowel-length criterion.
610.prule: One stress (with high pitch) per word: on the second syllable if it is closed by a non-glottal consonant in the underlying form; otherwise on the first syllable. Monosyllables (pronouns, clitics) are unstressed. Morpheme junctures do not affect the rule; the stress rules precede č->? and glottal/final-consonant deletion, so surface forms can be opaque (ma'pó 'clay' < mapop vs 'mápó 'head'; ka'ríwĩ < ka+rič+wĩ).
610.srule: None: one stress per word in Loos 1969 -- 'All other syllables are at this point [-stress]'; 'any syllable which is preceded by a stressed syllabic becomes unstressed'; 'the third syllable will have no stress or high pitch'. (Later metrical work builds disyllabic feet iteratively left to right and marks covert secondary heads, diagnosed by glottal-stop retention vs coalescence, Elias-Ulloa 2006: 158-159, 173-174; 'en capanahua no hay correlatos acústicos... para el acento secundario', González 2017: 130.)

It is therefore possible to insert the [word] juncture correctly in every case by placing it only before each formative." (T54, p.100); "The verb consisting of verb stem, aspectual and adverbial suffixes, person-marking and tense suffixes, and closure suffixes has a limit of three consecutive high pitches." (p.200). (The only prefix-like elements are undescribed body-part prefixes seen in a few examples, e.g. pi-čaʔčikin 'poke in the ribs', pi-rakaʔwɨ 'lie down on your back'.)

611.heavy: Vowel length: underlyingly long vowels count as two units in the odd/even count and an underlyingly long penult is always accented even if odd-numbered; an odd-numbered penult is accentable only if it can be lengthened (followed by a single consonant, vowel not A, not followed by H/glottal stop). Closed syllables (CC, H, glottal stop codas) are NOT heavy - they block accent on odd-numbered penults.
611.dflt: even-numbered penult accented; odd-numbered short unlengthenable penult -> antepenult; disyllables with unaccentable penult -> no accent or final accent
611.prule: Non-final (isolation/sentence-final) accent: count vowels from the word beginning (underlyingly long vowels and the a:- indef prefix count as two); an even-numbered penult is always accented (and lengthened if possible, i.e. unless followed by H, glottal stop or a vowel); an odd-numbered penult is accented (and lengthened) only if followed by a single consonant and its vowel is not A (exception, sec. 3.8 ex. 18: an odd-numbered penultimate A IS accented and lengthened when followed by a single W or Y, e.g. gá:yęˀ, sá:węh, hadihá:wiˀs); otherwise (vowel A before other consonants, CC cluster incl. T/K/J, or following H/glottal stop) the third-last vowel is accented; an underlyingly long penult is accented regardless of parity; accent shifts one vowel leftward across hiatus (only source of fourth-last accent). Two-vowel words whose penult is unaccentable are unaccented or finally accented. Mid-sentence words take final (continuing) accent.

evidence_works.detail: Cayuga, after Foster 1982, has stresses on even-numbered syllables from the left, with main stress on an even penult, on an odd heavy penult, and otherwise on the antepenult. The main-stress rule matches the catalog's parity-and-length statement from Dyck et al. 2024; the iterative even-syllable stresses add a secondary-stress claim the catalog's source does not make, since it describes one accent per word.

612.dq: For the most part stress can be determined by the phonological make-up of the word (Wolff 1972 sec. 3.0); also 'there is only one long vowel per word'.
612.dloc: Introduction, sec. 3.0 'Phonology' (stress paragraph; Gutenberg e-text); see also 3.21 (transcription of stress, ~529-538) and 5.11 'Shift of stress' (~653-686)
612.heavy: Long vowel (at most one per word, only in penult or final) takes stress wherever it stands; failing a long vowel, a CLOSED PENULT takes stress; an open short penult yields final stress. Closure is evaluated only for the penult ('stress is on the penultimate if it is closed'): a closed final never attracts stress (tan-aw [tánʔaw], tugnaw /túgnaw/ keep penult stress; inúm /ʔinúm/, sakay /sakáy/ are final-stressed by default, not by closure). So heavy = CVV in either window syllable, CVC in the penult only.
612.prule: (1) Stress falls on the long vowel if the word has one (nagdá [nagdā́], káun [kā́ʔun]); (2) with no long vowel, stress is on the penult if it is closed (tan-aw [tánʔaw], mugbù [múgbuʔ]); (3) if the penult is open and short, stress is on the ultimate (mala [malá]). 'Occasionally' a closed-penult word has final stress (mandǎr, dughǐt, marked with a wedge in the dictionary).
612.srule: Secondary stresses fall on alternate syllables to the left of the primary stress (rhythmic; weight-sensitivity of secondaries not stated). Not mentioned in Wolff 1972 (Introduction secs. 3.0, 3.21, 5.11 read); the statement is Shryock 1993's as digested by StressTyp2, corroborated first-hand by Bunye & Yap 1971 ('medial stress... generally occurs two syllables prior to the primary stress': magdàdaró 'farmer', mànanámbal 'doctor').
612.quote: Vowels may be long or short. Contrast between long and short vowels occurs only in the final and the penultimate syllable of the word: káun [kā́ʔun] ‘eat’ and nagdá [nagdā́] ‘is bringing’. Further, there is only one long vowel per word. There is also a phoneme of stress which has a very low contrastive function. For the most part stress can be determined by the phonological make-up of the word: 1 stress falls on the long vowel of the word if the word has a long vowel: nagdá [nagdā́], káun [kā́ʔun]. 2 for words that have no long vowel, stress is on the penultimate if it is closed: tan-aw [tánʔ…

morph.rootq: Wolff 1972 Intro sec 5.11 'Shift of stress': "The general rule is that an affixed form has the stress on the same syllable as the root alone. Where this general rule is broken, there is said to be SHIFT OF STRESS. When an affixed form has final stress where the root had penultimate stress, there is said to be SHIFT TO THE FINAL SYLLABLE ... kaun 'eat' + nag-(→) = nagkaun /nagkaʔún/ 'is eating'; tugnaw /túgnaw/ 'cold' + -un(→) = tugnawun /tugnawún/ 'be cold'." The basic word-level rule (sec 3.0) is purely phonological and does not mention the root: "stress falls on the long vowel of the word if the word has a long vowel ... for words that have no long vowel, stress is on the penultimate if…

The consultant produced every word for at least four times, first in isolation, next within the sentence frame, and then both repeated." morph.stmt: Cebuano is a root-and-affix language with heavy, predominantly prefixal verbal morphology plus a smaller set of voice/mood suffixes and circumfixes: Wolff 1972 sec 7.0 speaks of "the rich system of derivational and inflectional affixations to which Cebuano roots are subject, there are literally hundreds of different affixed forms for any given root", his sec 6.1 chart marks tense/voice/mode with prefixes (mu-, mi-, mag-, nag-, maka-, naka-, gi-, ma-, na-, i-) except future/subjunctive direct and local passives (-un, -a, -an, -i) and circumfixes (gi-...-an, ma-...-an), and the productive derivational bases…

613.dq: Basic word stress. In every word of more than one syllable, one of the syllables bears heavy stress ... In addition to word stress, there are stress patterns in sentences as well, which often have the effect of shifting the heavy stress off a word that would ordinarily receive it. The negative particle [ná], for example, always carries heavy stress in the sentence.
613.dloc: Ch. 2 'Pronunciation', sec. E 'Stress and Intonation', book pp. 24-27
613.heavy: Only a hedged native-vocabulary tendency: a word-final syllable that 'ends in a consonant' attracts stress (final closed syllable), otherwise penult; no vowel-length criterion is given; authors say the rule has 'as many exceptions... as there are words which follow it' and that stress location is 'not predictable'.
613.dflt: n/a (tendency only: penult when the final syllable is vowel-final)
613.prule: Location of heavy (primary) stress is not predictable and must be learned word by word; a native-word tendency (final if consonant-final, else penult) is stated but immediately hedged as having as many exceptions as adherents; loans keep donor stress; minimal pairs distinguished by stress alone (tánga/tangá, áspa/aspá, góra/gorá, kenastá/kénasta).
613.srule: Exists but unstudied; no placement given: 'there seem to be secondary stresses in Pashto as well as primary stresses... There are probably patterns of primary and secondary stresses in multi-syllabic words as well' (only impressionistic examples: [-ed-] in [wə́daredam] stronger than [-am]; first syllable of [akhistúnkay] stronger than 2nd/4th).
613.quote: Basic word stress. In every word of more than one syllable, one of the syllables bears heavy stress ... The location of the heavy stress (whether on the last syllable, the next-to-last, or one of the earlier syllables) is not predictable in Pashto, and the spelling system does not mark stress at all. To ascertain where the heavy stress is in a Pashto word, the non-native speaker must ask a native speaker how to pronounce the word, and then listen for the stressed syllable. The stress in native Pashto words is generally on the last syllable if the syllable ends in a consonant, and on the next-…

evidence_works.work: Trofimov 2023, O pravilakh udareniia v imennykh osnovakh pushtu [On the rules of stress in Pashto nominal stems] (Journal of Language Relationship 21(3-4): 224-241)
evidence_works.note: Historical-etymological study; no elicitation. Its synchronic stress data are dictionary stress marks (Aslanov 1985 PRS, Zudin 1950 KARS, Lebedev 1973 RASP, Morgenstierne 2003 NEVP) and the counts of Becka 1969 (one fifth of Aslanov's dictionary). Agrees that Pashto stress is free and variable in place (p.224: 'Iazyk pushtu kharakterizuetsia raznomestnym svobodnym udareniem'). Adds a quantified default: 68.3% of all words have or tend to final stress (p.228, citing Becka 1969: 57-58); abstract p.241: 'the vast majority of modern Pashto forms have stress on the final syllable'. Sharpens the entry's vowel-final tendency by vowel quality: every word ending in -ə is stressed on that vowel (p.231: 'Absoliutno vse slova, imeiushchie okonchanie -ə, imeiut udarenie na dannoi foneme'; p.236: unstressed final zwarakay 'v printsipe iskliuchen' in nominal stems), final -ə́y and long -ā always take final stress (pp.237, 239), while -a and -ay split about evenly in Aslanov's dictionary (139 stressed vs 168 unstressed -a; 99 stressed vs 90 unstressed -ay; p.228 quoting Becka 1969: 95). Archaic Proto-Iranian barytone vs oxytone contrast survives in *ā-stems (áspa etc.) and -ay < *-a-ka stems (p.239). Says nothing about secondary stress.

614.dq: Stress in Bikol is phonemic and contrastive: dapít 'regarding', dápit 'to escort the dead (priests)'. Once the stress on the root word is known, then the placement of other stresses due to affixation can be predicted.
614.dloc: Mintz 2000 p. 91, section 'Orthography and Basic Phonology', stress paragraph (Rosetta scan p. 2)
614.heavy: No weight criterion stated in the sources opened. The only weight-like statement is the StressTyp2 carried passage attributed to Mintz & Britanico 1985 ('Only if both syllables in the word are closed the stress predictably falls on the final syllable'), i.e. closed syllable (CVC); not verified (1985 dictionary section 3 unreachable). Mintz 1971 p. 18 says reduplicated CVC-CVC bases (KÚLKÚL, PÚKPÚK) carry stress 'equally on both' parts.
614.dflt: not applicable (no weight rule); root stress lexically penultimate or final
614.prule: Root stress is phonemic/contrastive (final vs penultimate on disyllabic roots; minimal pairs dapít/dápit, kuyóg/kúyog); given root stress, affixal stress is predictable: suffixation shifts stress one syllable rightward (verbs); for derived nouns/adjectives penult root stress moves to the final syllable and final root stress stays put.
614.srule: In prefixed and CV-reduplicated forms a further stress (Mintz: 'a primary stress') falls on every second syllable counting leftward from the lexical stress of the base (ta'ó > íta'ó > itáta'ó > ítináta'ó; apód > nagáapód); none if fewer than two syllables precede the base stress (húgas > huhúgas); the count is made from the base stress before any suffixal shift (áapodón, súsubli'ón). quantity-insensitive; relative prominence of root vs rhythmic stresses not stated.
614.quote: [Mintz 2000:91] Bikol is a syllable-timed language. This means that each syllable in an utterance takes approximately the same amount of time to pronounce. (Miyaoka's culminative peak is defined over the pause-bou…
615.dloc: Jacobson 1985: p.25 (light/heavy definitions), p.30 (NSU remark on 'secondary' stress), p.33 (General Central Yupik rules 1-7); Miyaoka 1985: p.53 sec. 2.1 (phonological unit), p.55 sec. 3.1 (unit-final accent; rhythmic vs regressive accent), p.56 sec. 3.2 (culmination); Krauss Introduction sec. 2
615.heavy: 'Heavy' = a syllable with two vowels (long vowel or two-vowel cluster: CVV, CVVC); heavy syllables are inherently stressed anywhere. Closed syllables (CVC) count only by position: a word-INITIAL closed syllable is stressed (ICSS), and in General Central Yupik a closed syllable before an open light non-final syllable is stressed (regressive stress). Reduced vowel e vs full a/i/u matters for lengthening/gemination, not for weight.
615.dflt: All-light words: stress on even-numbered syllables counting from the left (2nd, 4th...), never on the final syllable; e.g. NSU qayapigkani 'his own future authentic kayak' with rhythmic stress and lengthening on -ya- and -ka-.
615.prule: Main prominence IS ranked by Miyaoka (1985:55, sec. 3.1): 'If a phonological unit has two or more accented syllables, the one closest to the end of the unit carries the greatest prominence. This is called "unit-final" accent' (p.56: 'the culmination of prominence with the longest duration, the greatest stress, and the highest tone'). So primary = the RIGHTMOST accented syllable of the word/phonological unit, whose position is fixed by the weight-sensitive left-to-right iambic parse (heavy = two-vowel syllables stressed anywhere; word-initial closed syllable stressed; GCY regressive stress on a closed syllable before a light open non-final syllable) plus word-final de-stressing -- normally the penult or antepenult, never lexically chosen. Jacobson (1985:30) treats all stresses as phonetically alike and ranks none.
615.srule: All non-rightmost stresses of the same parse (Miyaoka 1985 Rules I-IV = Jacobson 1985 rules 2-4, 7): the word-initial syllable if closed; every heavy (two-vowel) syllable; iambic rhythmic stress on every second syllable counting from the left (the syllable after an unstressed one); regressive stress on a closed syllable before a light open non-final syllable (GCY) and on the syllable before a heavy syllable; never the word-final syllable. All-open-syllable words: even-numbered non-final syllables; all-closed words: odd-numbered non-final syllables. Per Jacobson these stresses 'sound the same as any other stress'; Alden 2023 finds no acoustic primary/secondary difference at all.

616.dloc: Jacobson 1985:25-26 (sec. 1, 2.1); Krauss 1985:21; Krauss 1985:48 sec. 2 (ERIC ED398761 PDF frames 34-35, 31, 56)
616.heavy: heavy = syllable with two vowels (long vowel; SY has no unlike-vowel clusters); light = one vowel. Closed syllables explicitly do NOT attract stress ('not affected by whether any syllables are open or closed, not even the word-initial syllable', Krauss 1985:21; Jacobson brackets 'Initial closed syllable stress' as inapplicable to SY). Reduced vowel e blocks rhythmic lengthening but not stress.
616.dflt: stress on 2nd, 4th... syllables counting from the word beginning, never the final syllable (e.g. qayapigkani [qaya:pixka:ni], angyaghllaka with stress on -yagh- only)
616.prule: No primary/secondary distinction: inherent stress on every heavy (CVV) syllable; rhythmic stress on any syllable following an unstressed syllable (alternating from word start or from the last stressed syllable); word-final syllable de-stressed. Krauss 1985:48: no higher-level hierarchy among the word's stresses ('Evidence for this is negative').
616.srule: No primary/secondary ranking: all stresses in the word are of equal degree (no main stress; Krauss 1985:48 finds the evidence for any higher-level hierarchy among the word's stresses 'negative'). Every stress is placed by the general rule: each heavy (CVV) syllable, plus each syllable following an unstressed syllable (binary alternation rightward from the word start and from each stressed syllable), the final syllable never stressed.

Rhythmic stress: The syllable following an unstressed syllable is stressed; 4. In SY the stem-stress principle is served by the following Initial Syllable Lengthening Rule (ISL): The vowel (if full) of the initial syllable…
morph.elicq: Jacobson 1985:25 n.2 states only the consultants ('Information on SY is from Linda Badten and Vera Kaneshiro of Gambell and others from both Gambell and Savoonga') and illustrates the rules with single words in phonetic transcription (method otherwise unstated). Krauss 1985:49-50 (same volume, same speakers) explicitly contrasts isolated words with words in construction and connected speech: 'nenglu ... [pronounced] in isolation ... there is, at any rate, an underlying prosodic difference still potentially realizable in construction with other words'; 'the tonal contour of ordinary disyllables ... in isolation, proves to be different ... in construction ... thus aghnaq una \'that woman\''…
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and polysynthetic: 'The structure of the CSY word, and actually for the word in all Eskimo languages, is described by the following formula... base + postbases + ending + enclitics... Postbases are derivational suffixes; the ending is a morphologically simple or complex unit, and functions as an inflectional suffix' (de Reuse 1988:34-35); the only exception is the demonstrative anaphoric prefix: demonstratives 'are unique in that they may contain the only prefix of the language' (de Reuse 1988:41; cf. Jacobson 1985:28 'ta- (the only prefix in the language)').

tn.quote: Stress must be characterized at this stage mainly by greater energy, volume, and especially, higher pitch. … Duration is not the only phonetic feature that distinguishes them, however. An equally important distinguishing characteristic is the tonal contour. Both types start, as do all stressed vowels, with a relatively high pitch and energy level. … In an overlong vowel there is usually a noticeable falling of the pitch and energy level … Perceptually, then, it would seem that both duration and tonal contour are significant for distinguishing long from overlong vowels.

tn.note: No tone phonemes are posited: prosody is stress plus vowel lengthening; higher pitch marks stressed vowels, and a falling vs flat contour is a secondary cue to overlong vs long stressed vowels. Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): number of tones not stated -> 0 (sec. 2 'Phonology', proof p. 8).

617.dq: In the Miwok word there is one syllable which bears a fixed stress that is not lost or appreciably diminished in connected speech. (Freeland 1951:7)
617.dloc: Freeland 1951 §6 p.6 (syllable length), §7.1 p.7 (major stress), §7.2 pp.7-8 (secondary stress), §7.3 pp.8-9 ('Potential stress': disyllables with no long syllable) [HathiTrust uc1.31210001229770 seq 20-23, page = seq-14]; Hayes 1995:112-113, 261
617.heavy: LONG syllable = contains a long vowel, or a short vowel followed by a long consonant or by a combination of two consonants; two lengths only, LONG and SHORT. Freeland's table (p.6) counts CV and word-FINAL CVC (short consonant) as SHORT, and as LONG: CVC before another consonant, CV + long consonant, CVV, and final CVVC — so CVV and non-final closed CVC are heavy, but a final CVC closed by a single short consonant is light (hence CVCVʔ disyllables like nakèʔ 'end', šalàʔ 'feather' have 'no intrinsically long syllable', §7.3) (Freeland 1951:6, 8).
617.dflt: Does not arise in words of 3+ syllables per Freeland (second syllable is long whenever the first is short); disyllabic stems with no intrinsically long syllable: secondary stress on the final syllable in isolation, either syllable or no stress in connected speech (Freeland 1951:8; Hayes 1995:112-113 'unstressable words').
617.prule: One fixed 'major stress' per word, always on the first or second syllable and always on a long syllable: if the first syllable is long it is stressed (even if the second is also long); in words of three or more syllables with a short first syllable the second syllable is long and stressed (Freeland 1951:7).
617.srule: Secondary stresses occur (they tend to disappear in running narrative) and fall most frequently on the word-final syllable: three-syllable nouns with initial major stress and longer nouns normally have a final secondary stress; three-syllable nouns with major stress on the second syllable have none, and a final case suffix is unstressed. Three-syllable verb forms with initial major stress have a final secondary stress; longer verb forms usually stress a final syllabic pronominal suffix, otherwise certain suffix syllables (distant past -ànï-, usitative -ìšï-, -tànï- 'to try to'). A secondary stress on the syllable right after the major stress is not usual (only vocatives and volitionals).

All those syllables are LONG which contain a long vowel, or a short vowel that is followed by a long consonant, or a combination of two consonants. ... [p.7] 7.1. Major stress. Phonograph records were made and analyzed with his help, and special attention was given to the phonetic, and particularly the rhythmic, features of the language. In this work of phonetic analysis I was fortunate enough to have the help of H. J. Uldall'. §7.1 p.7: 'a fixed stress that is not lost or appreciably diminished in connected speech'. §7.2 p.7: 'Secondary stresses occur, and in short phrases and conversational sentences they are quite noticeable, but they tend to disappear in running narrative.' §7.3 p.8: 'When these words are spoken alone there is a secondary stress on the last syllable. ...…
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing with extensive stem-internal prosodic alternation: 'Of these processes, the two outstanding ones are suffixation and prosodic change.' with footnote 11 'Other incremental changes are conspicuously lacking. Prefixation and infixation are not used. Stem composition is not an active process' (§9-10 p.10); '§38... Since there is no prefixation in Miwok, the first position in any verb form is occupied by the stem.... Stem ± adverbial element + tense element ± obj. pronominal element + subj. pronominal element + case element ± post-clitic.' (pp.92-93); 'the total absence of prefixation in any dialect' (p.147 fn.145).

618.caution: Based on an excerpt only; the full text of the source has not been consulted.
618.dq: For nearly all Choctaw nouns, accent falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable. ... However, the accent on underived nouns is not predictable. (Broadwell 2006:17-18)
618.dloc: Broadwell 2006 pp. 17-18, 21 (Google Books search-within excerpt, vol. id UBvJKMRtfe4C); Lombardi & McCarthy 1991 ms pp. 5-6, 10-11 (sec. 3.2 Foot Structure)
618.heavy: Bimoraic syllables = closed (CVC) and long-vowel (CVV) syllables (Broadwell 2006:17 'Rules that distinguish between monomoraic and bimoraic syllables (e.g., rhythmic lengthening)'; Lombardi & McCarthy 1991:5-6 'Regularities like these are familiar from languages where CVC and CVV syllables are heavy'; nasal vowels phonetically long and pattern as bimoraic). Weight conditions the iambic rhythmic-lengthening parse only; it is not stated to condition pitch-accent placement.
618.dflt: not applicable to accent placement (accent is final or penult by lexical/morphological class regardless of weight); in the rhythmic parse an all-light word lengthens even-numbered nonfinal syllables counting from the left
618.prule: Word prominence is a pitch accent (high pitch), not stress. In nouns the accent falls on the final or the penultimate syllable (one noun with antepenultimate accent); which of the two is NOT predictable for underived nouns (near-minimal pairs Chahta'/bahta', nanih/nani'); deverbal nominalizations have predictable penult accent; verbs normally have final accent (tense markers accented when word-final, with complications when further morphemes follow).
618.srule: No stress prominence reported ('stress prominence does not seem to be a feature of Choctaw phonetics'); rhythm is iambic and realized as vowel LENGTH: quantity-sensitive iambs left to right (CVV, CVC heavy); every even-numbered nonfinal CV syllable in a run of light syllables lengthens; a heavy syllable restarts the count; final syllables never lengthen. Whether foot heads carry stress cues is uninvestigated instrumentally (Gordon & Martin 2023:281).
618.quote: [Broadwell 2006:17-18, snippets] ... pitch accent language, but there seem to be almost no pairs which are distinguished by pitch alone. 618.tone: Pitch accent realized as high tone ('The acute accent marks a high tone; low-toned syllables are unmarked. Only some Choctaw words have an accent.' Lombardi & McCarthy 1991 fn. 1; 'accent in Choctaw is an unpredictable property of some words or morphological patterns. It is realized by high tone.' ibid. ms p. 30, after Nicklas 1974:12). Broadwell 2006:17 (sec. 2.2 'Pitch accent', excerpt): '... pitch accent language, but there seem to be almost no pairs which are distinguished by pitch alone' (one minimal pair tanáp 'war' / tánap 'turnip', the latter an English loan); noun accent final or penult, not predictable for underived nouns; penult accent on deverbal nominalizations (pp. 18, 52); in verbs accent tied to tense markers (p. 18 ex. 8a-b) and verb grades add pitch accent within the verb stem (p. 161); pitch accent written only on nonfinal syllables. Stress prominence 'does not seem to be a feature of Choctaw phonetics' (L&M ms p. 10); rhythm surfaces as iambic vowel lengthening only.

619.caution: Based on an excerpt only; the full text of the source has not been consulted.
619.dq: Although the accent does not occur on any fixed syllable as in some languages, it is as far towards the end of the word as the following rules allow. (Krueger 1961: 86; contrasted with p. 87 phrase accent: 'In a few set phrases, usually of a noun plus a functional word such as a postposition or particle, there may be only one accent, or else a weakened secondary accent.')
619.dloc: Krueger 1961 pp. 86-88 (section 1.3 'Accent': opening paragraph p. 86, before 1.31; set-phrase accent p. 87); Dobrovolsky 1999 p. 539, p. 542
619.heavy: full (non-reduced) vowel: any vowel other than the reduced vowel phonemes /ě/ and /ǎ/; a syllable with a reduced vowel repels the accent (Krueger 1961: 71-72 'reduced, and can occur stressed only in the first syllable')
619.dflt: initial syllable (Krueger 1961: 86; Hayes 1981 carried quote); Dobrovolsky 1999 argues phonetically that all-reduced words carry no stress at all and the perceived initial 'default stress' is an early intonational F0 fall; he also reports a South Chuvashia dialect where the default is right-edge.
619.prule: Accent falls as far toward the end of the word as possible: on the last syllable unless it contains a reduced vowel /ě, ǎ/; otherwise on the syllable immediately preceding the run of final reduced-vowel syllables, i.e. on the last full vowel; when every syllable has a reduced vowel the accent is on the first syllable (examples /tắtămăr/, /śávărănătămărččě/; Dobrovolsky 1999: 'stress the last full vowel of a word; if there are no full vowels, stress the first vowel of the word').
619.srule: None word-internally: Krueger 1961 (pp. 86-88, section 1.3) assigns one accent per word and mentions a secondary accent only in intensifying reduplication (/šáp-šurǎ/ 'snow-white': particle primary, adjective 'may have a secondary stress') and in set phrases of noun + postposition/particle (p. 87). Dobrovolsky 1999: 542 states that Chuvash 'displays a layer of rhythmic stresses' but gives no placement ('worth a study of its own').
619.quote: ... accent in Chuvash is phonologically irrelevant, since its placement or misplacement does not create a different word . Al- though the accent does not occur on any fixed syllable as in some languages, it is as far towards the end of the word as the following rules allow . morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing and agglutinative: 'Nouns get suffixes in the following order: derivation+ possessive+ number+ case. e.g. kuś+lăχ+ămăr+sem+pe ‘with our glasses’' (Róna-Tas 2007 §1.5.2), and verbs take negation, tense, mood and person as suffixes (§1.5.8–1.5.9); the only preposed grammatical material is the free prohibitive particle an ('an (before verb)', §1.5.8; 'an kala ‘don’t speak’', §3.10.1) and reduplicative intensifier syllables such as šap-šură 'snow-white', which Krueger 1961: 128 flags as exceptional ('note prefix!'); interrogative and additive markers are enclitics (=i, =te).

620.dq: The most common position for stress is the first syllable of the word. (Charney 1993, ch. 2 opening page)
620.dloc: Charney 1993 ch. 2 'Phonology' first page + Table 2.1 (Rosetta excerpt, open); Charney 1993:40-44 (StressTyp2 carried); Osborn & Smalley 1949:95 (StressTyp2 carried)
620.heavy: Secondary stress is counted in morae ('every second mora rightward'), so a long vowel (two morae) is what makes a syllable count double; diphthongs ai/oi/ui count as one mora (Charney via Wikipedia). Closed syllables (codas are mostly /h/) are not mentioned as heavy. StressTyp2 renders this as 'secondary stress on all heavy syllables'.
620.dflt: Primary initial; in all-light words secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables counting from the left (every second mora = every second syllable).
620.prule: Primary stress on the first syllable of the word (quantity-insensitive), with lexically marked exceptions: loans, some words with non-initial long vowels, animal/plant names ending in a stressed long vowel, and a few doubly-stressed words; non-initial stress is written with an acute.
620.srule: Secondary stress on every second mora counting rightward from the primary stress (a long vowel counts two morae), e.g. [wahatimatòʔikatɨ] 'twelve'; also described as secondary stress 'on every other vowel following' the stressed syllable (it blocks devoicing of that vowel).
620.quote: [Charney 1993, ch. 2 opening, open] "Vowels occur in three surface forms: short, long, and voiceless. Voiceless vowels arise from short, unstressed vowels. morph.elicq: No statement of how stress was determined is visible in the accessible parts of Charney 1993 (ch.2 opening; pp.32, 40, 42, 43 snippets): "Primary stress is always marked in this work when it is noninitial" (p.40); "secondary stress is placed on every second mora rightward. morph.stmt: Comanche is predominantly suffixing in inflection and derivation (case, number, aspect/mood, nominalizers, benefactive-causative -ki, verbalizers, diminutive are all suffixes; Charney 1993:6/113: transitivity and derivation are handled by "the instrumental prefixes (which form a rich system), the unspecified argument prefixes, the benefactive/causative marker, and by nominalizing the verb... 621.heavy: long vowels only ('every syllable which surfaces with a long vowel'; ST1: long vowels; initial stress 'regardless of weight'); closed syllables not counted as heavy (closed 'lum' in ˈdjalumˈbaːdaŋˈbeː is unstressed)
621.prule: Stress on the initial syllable and on every long-vowel syllable; when a light initial syllable is followed by a heavy (CVV) second syllable the initial stress is dropped and stress falls on the second syllable: optionally in disyllables (ˈdjuluːn ~ djuˈluːn), obligatorily in words of three or more syllables (yaˈgaːla, not *ˈyagaːla; ŋaˈmaːla, not *ˈŋamaːla). Main and secondary stresses are described as equally prominent (Rice 1992:64; Goedemans NMS type).
621.srule: All stresses are reported equally prominent (no main/secondary distinction, NMS). Besides the initial, stress falls on every syllable that surfaces with a long vowel (CVV), placed by weight rather than by count: up to three unstressed light syllables may precede a heavy (ˈgawařiˈwaːla, ˈmandaˈřaːm) and non-initial light syllables are never stressed (ˈgabalŋinj); in a string of adjacent long-vowel syllables only the odd-numbered keep length and stress (ˈdjalumˈbaːdaŋˈbeː).
621.quote: Stress occurs on the first syllable regardless of weight, and on every syllable which surfaces with a long vowel (Rice 1992, 63-65). morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing: Sharpe 1998:23, endorsing Livingstone (1892) for the whole dialect chain -- 'It is well known that the Australian dialects are agglutinative, everything in the nature of inflection being obtained by suffixes... As we know now, some Australian languages also have prefixes, but he is certainly right about Yugambeh and other dialects of the language. Because suffixes can show who is doing what to what, with what, and where, word order is more variable than in English'; for Gidabal proper, Geytenbeek 1971 (as summarised via Sharpe 2005): 'Verbs are conjugated with the use of suffixes... Verb suffixes are placed in six orders', nouns take ordered case/gender/number…

corr.detail: StressTyp2 entry: "Hanis Coos: primary stress: StressTyp2 code LEX (lexical) (P); no secondary stress". The source gives: Every non-clitic word bears a stress accent, but the stress accent 'is not inseparably associated with any particular syllable' and 'may... be shifted freely from one syllable to another'; no placement rule is given. A second, rising-tone ('circumflex') accent 'appears mostly on the last syllable' and contrasts lexically with stress in at least one stem pair (he'laq 'arrive' vs helâq 'climb up'). — StressTyp2 codes primary 'LEX (P)' and carries the same p. 309 passage; the LEX part matches Frachtenberg, but the penultimate default ('(P)') is the StressTyp2 compiler's…

622.tone: Two accent types: besides the stress accent (acute), a 'rising tone' (circumflex ^) that 'appears mostly on the last syllable, and may best be compared with the intonation given to the word so in the English interrogative sentence Is that so ?'; the two contrast in one stem pair, he'laq 'to get, to arrive' (stress accent) vs helâq 'to climb up' (rising tone on a). No further tone system is described (Frachtenberg 1922 sec. 5 p. 309).

tn.quote: With the exception of the monosyllabic particles, that are either enclitic or proclitic, each word in Coos has its stress accent, designated by the acute mark (') or by the rising tone rendered here by ~. ... 623.dq: (16a) STRESS: Every full word in Creek bears stress. In the simplest pattern, iambic feet are assigned left-to-right. Word-level stress (') is assigned to the last foot and is associated with the value H.
623.heavy: Light syllables are 'those that end in short vowels' (Haas 1977a:196, cited fn. 4); heavy = syllables with a long vowel or closed by a consonant (CVV, CVC).
623.dflt: All-light word: level tone accent on the last even-numbered syllable counting from the left (final if syllable count even, penult if odd).
623.prule: Nonfinite forms (nouns, infinitives, etc.; placement 'generally predictable', 'largely automatic'): left-to-right iambic feet (L'X) or ('H); word-level stress (Haas's level tone accent, realized as high pitch H) on the head of the last foot (End Rule Right): ultima if heavy ('normally'; the durative suffix -i: is outside the stress domain), penult if penult heavy and ultima light, otherwise the last even-numbered light syllable counting from the word start or from the last heavy syllable. Finite verbs: level/falling/rising accents mark aspectual grades on the stem-final syllable and some affixes have inherent accent, so placement there is morphological (Haas 1977a:202, 204: placement automatic only in words made up of morphemes with no fixed accent; with a heavy ultima 'no longer automatic').
623.srule: Secondary stress on the heads of the nonfinal iambic feet built left to right (second syllable of a light-initial disyllabic foot, or a heavy syllable footed alone); the last foot's head carries primary stress. The authors argue the nonfinal feet are real and note 'a few minimal contrasts in secondary stress' (fn. 6), with a fuller account deferred to Martin (in progress).
623.quote: Nonfinite forms ... The placement of this accent is generally predictable, described by Haas (1977a:202-4) in the following terms: (3a) In a string of light syllables containing no fixed accents, level tone will be placed on the last even-numbered syllable ... (3b) If the penult is a heavy syllable and the ultima is light, level tone will be placed on the penult ... (3c) In a string of light syllables following a heavy syllable, level tone will be placed on the last even-numbered syllable ... (3d) If the ultima is heavy, level tone will normally be placed on that syllable ... [fn.4] Haas (197…
623.idn: the Muskogee dialect of Creek (Haas 1977a: 'Creek or Muskogee language', Oklahoma, old Creek Nation); data: MJ02 p. 33: eight native speakers of the Muskogee dialect (four women, four men, ages early fifties to late eighties), recorded in groups of two to four with Margaret Mauldin (University of Oklahoma) prompting…
623.exq_: The placement of this accent is generally predictable ... [fn. 3] A handful of nouns (e.g., nâ:ki 'something') have falling tone accent. ... (3d) If the ultima is heavy, level tone will normally be placed on that syllable [fn. 5] ... The durative suffix -i: in 'white' is outside the domain of the s…
623.tone: The primary source analyses Creek as having stress AND tone: 'In our view, Creek is a language with stress (´), falling tone (^), and rising tone (ˇ). Three distinct phonological phenomena-stress, tone, and intonation-interact to shape word prosody' (Martin & Johnson 2002:47). Stress = Haas's (1977a) 'level tone accent', cued by pitch (H on the word-level stressed syllable, leftward spreading, downstep between stress domains), not by duration; falling and rising tones occur chiefly on finite verbs marking aspectual grades, falling tone also on 'a handful of nouns (e.g., nâ:ki 'something')' (fn. 3). Haas 1977a describes the whole system as 'tonal accent' (key syllables with level, falling or extra-high/rising tone, downward drift between successive key syllables).

624.dq: La sílaba acentuada ... es la primera sílaba con tono alto en una palabra fonológica ... el acento primario cae siempre en una de las cuatro primeras sílabas.
624.dloc: §2.3 'Sílaba, tono y acento', pp. 6-7; §3.3 'Desplazamiento del acento', pp. 13-14 (19-20)
624.heavy: No syllable-weight criterion: syllables are strictly (C)V (no long vowels, no codas). StressTyp's 'heavy' = high tone, i.e. the accented syllable is defined as the first high-toned syllable of the phonological word; separately, non-high vowels of certain suffixes (-A plural/past, -O causative, abstract nominalizer) attract the accent one syllable rightward (vowel quality, morphophonological).
624.dflt: unstated (source gives no rule for words without a high tone; StressTyp2 notes the same gap)
624.prule: Accent falls on the first high-toned syllable of the phonological word; its position is lexically contrastive (/kuˈjɑwɨ/ 'I bathed' vs /ˈkujɑwɨ/ 'I ran'), most often the second syllable, always within the first four syllables. Accented vowels are slightly longer.
624.srule: Rhythmic secondary stress on every second syllable to the right of the primary stress: iambic feet parsed left-to-right from the primary-stressed syllable, every foot head after the first bearing secondary stress (default σˈσσˌσσˌσ, lexically initial-stressed ˈσσˌσσˌσσ); in compounds each stem is its own domain and the stresses of non-initial stems are secondary.
624.quote: En cubeo una sílaba consta de (C)V. Contrastan dos niveles de tono, bajo ... y alto ... La sílaba acentuada, (marcada con [ˈ] antes de la sílaba acentuada en los ejemplos fonéticos de esta sección) es la primera sílaba con tono alto en una palabra fonológica. En la mayoría de las palabras cubeas, ésta es la segunda sílaba de la palabra, y el acento primario cae siempre en una de las cuatro primeras sílabas. El acento (equivalentemente, la posición de la primera sílaba con tono alto) es contrastivo, por ejemplo: (19) /kuˈjɑwɨ/ 'me bañé (recientemente)' /ˈkujɑwɨ/ 'corrí (recientemente)'. Además…
624.loc: §2.3 'Sílaba, tono y acento', pp. 6-7; §3.3 'Desplazamiento del acento', pp. 13-14 (19-20)
624.idn: cubeo (la lengua cubea), all three river areas; no single dialect singled out; data: Speakers of Cubeo from the Vaupés, Querarí and Cuduyarí rivers (Departamento del Vaupés, SE Colombia); fieldwork by J. K. & Neva Salser 1964-1976, Nancy L. Morse 1980-1990s, Judith Ferguson 1984-1986 (Instituto Lingüístico de Verano)
624.exq_: En la mayoría de las palabras cubeas, ésta es la segunda sílaba de la palabra, y el acento primario cae siempre en una de las cuatro primeras sílabas. El acento (equivalentemente, la posición de la primera sílaba con tono alto) es contrastivo
624.tone: Two contrastive tone levels, high vs low (low realized mid or low): /kábṹká/ 'oreja' vs /kábãve/ 'antorcha', /xã́jɨbU/ 'estoy mirando' vs /xãjɨ́bU/ 'me doy un topetón con'. The accented syllable is defined as the first high-toned syllable of the phonological word, so accent position and the position of the first H tone are one and the same contrast; accented vowels are also slightly longer. Tone is not marked outside §2.3.

morph.rootq: Main statement is over the phonological word, not the root: 'La sílaba acentuada ... es la primera sílaba con tono alto en una palabra fonológica. En la mayoría de las palabras cubeas, ésta es la segunda sílaba de la palabra, y el acento primario cae siempre en una de las cuatro primeras sílabas. El acento ... es contrastivo' (§2.3, pp.6-7). But the morphophonology treats accent as a property of the root that specific suffixes can pull rightward: 'Las vocales no altas atraen el acento primario de una palabra desde una vocal acentuada inmediatamente precedente ... Un ejemplo de esto son las raíces de sustantivos de dos sílabas que se pluralizan con la adición del sufijo -A: /pɨˈrɨ/ mano…
morph.elicq: No elicitation method is stated for the accent description; the section cites the earlier SIL phonology ('(J. K. Salser, 1976)', §2.3 p.6) and refers only to speech style: 'Además de la diferencia en tono, las vocales acentuadas son ligeramente más largas que las inacentuadas en el habla normal, y significativamente alargadas en el habla enfática.' (§2.3, p.7). Data provenance in general: 'El material para este trabajo fue recogido por J. K. y Neva Salser (1964-1976), Nancy L. Morse (1980 hasta el presente) y Judith Ferguson (1984-1986) ... Los datos fueron facilitados por hablantes de cubeo de los ríos Vaupés, Querarí y Cuduyarí.' (§1, p.2).
morph.stmt: Overwhelmingly suffixing: 'Todos los afijos verbales del cubeo son sufijos, con la excepción de los direccionales: xa- "fuera del hablante" y da- "hacia el hablante".' (§4.2, p.19); nominal morphology (classifiers, gender/number, plural, diminutive, case) is likewise suffixal, the only prefixes listed in Apéndice 1 'Prefijos' (p.179) being the demonstratives (i-, ãdi-, di-, ape-), ta- 'cuál' and the possessive prefixes used with kinship terms (xi-, bɨ-, ĩ-, dẽ-, jɨxe-, etc.).

tn.quote: En cubeo una sílaba consta de (C)V. Contrastan dos niveles de tono, bajo (sin marcar en los ejemplos fonémicos) y alto (marcado con acento agudo sobre la vocal en los ejemplos de esta sección): /kábṹká/ ‘oreja’, y /kábãve/ ‘antorcha’; /xã́jɨbU/ ‘estoy mirando’, y /xãjɨ́bU/ ‘me doy un topetón con’. El tono bajo tiene dos variantes, medio … y bajo … La sílaba acentuada … es la primera sílaba con tono alto en una palabra fonológica. … El acento (equivalentemente, la posición de la primera sílaba con tono alto) es contrastivo
tn.translation: In Cubeo a syllable consists of (C)V. Two tone levels contrast, low (unmarked in the phonemic examples) and high (marked with an acute accent over the vowel in the examples of this section): /kábṹká/ 'ear' vs /kábãve/ 'torch'; /xã́jɨbU/ 'I am looking' vs /xãjɨ́bU/ 'I bump into'. The low tone has two variants, mid ... and low ... The accented syllable ... is the first syllable with high tone in a phonological word. ... The accent (equivalently, the position of the first high-toned syllable) is contrastive
tn.cite: Morse, Nancy L. & Michael B. Maxwell. 1999. Gramática del cubeo. Traductor: Bernardo Montes (Spanish edition of Cubeo Grammar, Studies in the Languages of Colombia 5 / SIL-UTA Publications in Linguistics 130, 1999). Primera edición. Santafé de Bogotá: Editorial Alberto Lleras Camargo. 194 pp. ISBN 958-9281-29-X. SIL archive entry 19056.

tn.note: Two contrastive level tones, high and low (low surfaces as mid or low); the accent is the first high-toned syllable of the word, within the first four syllables; accented vowels are slightly longer.

624.cfw: Morse & Maxwell (1999/2000) and Chacon (2012) both describe Cubeo main stress as lexically contrastive with a second-syllable default, differing only on the window and on whether stress is simply the first high tone.

evidence_works.work: Chacon 2011, The interaction of stress and tones in Kubeo (Working Papers in Linguistics, University of Hawai'i at Mānoa 42(2): 1-21; PDF is 23 pp. including two front-matter pages; stress section 2 pp. 1-10, section 3 'Tones' from p. 11, summary section 4 pp. 18-19)
evidence_works.detail: Preliminary version of the analysis the entry already names from Chacon 2012 (sec_loc: ch. 4 §4.1.1 pp. 117-119, §4.1.2.3 p. 134; cfw). Primary stress: 'In no word in Kubeo can stress fall after the second syllable counting from the left' (p. 4); 'Stress is free in the sense that it can fall on any of the first two syllables' and 'stress is not quantity-sensitive in Kubeo' (p. 5); 'stress falling on the second syllable of words is the default case and stress on the first syllable of words is the exceptional case', with first-syllable stress 'specified in the underlying structure of lexical morphemes' (p. 6). Secondary stress: 'one perceives a rhythmic alternation affecting every other syllable from the location of the stressed syllable, which gives the perception of secondary stress' (p. 6, Table 1); 'Primary stress is always on the left-most stressed syllable in a word, and secondary stress is always on the subsequent stressed syllables to the right' (p. 7); the stem is the foot-parsing domain in compounds (p. 7). Phonetic cues (acoustic sample of 80 words, Table 2 p. 8): 'Duration, which makes the stressed syllable the longest one in the word, is the most common and consistent indication of prominence in Kubeo', pitch less reliable because of up-step and down-step, intensity 'not a good correlate' (p. 8); secondary stressed syllables 'can be marked by longer duration than unstressed syllables' and are 'less audible in word-final position' (p. 9). The two-syllable window (vs Morse & Maxwell's 'una de las cuatro primeras sílabas') and the tone-vs-stress separation are the same differences the entry's cfw already records for Chacon 2012; the entry's kind=lexical and second-syllable default are matched.

625.heavy: No weight criterion in either source. Silva 2012: feet are bimoraic, stress on the second mora; 'There is no closed syllable in the language'; (C)Vʔ/(C)Vh syllables 'are not stressed'. Miller 1999 (ST1 note): heavy-for-stress = lexical marking.
625.dflt: n/a (no weight); Silva: second mora of the word/root
625.prule: Miller 1999: stress phonemic (lexical); stressed syllable has high pitch; stems have primary, secondary or no stress, stressless stems throw stress onto a suffix (pitch-accent analysis after Barnes 1996 Tuyuca, per Silva 2012:24). Silva 2012: mixed stress-tone system; duration-cued stress is predictable - iambic bimoraic feet parsed left-to-right, primary stress on the last (second) mora of the root = leftmost foot head (word layer left-headed); verb roots stressed only once suffixed; (C)Vʔ/(C)Vh syllables never stressed; the lexically contrastive prominence is tone (H vs L; four surface melodies H, HL, LH, L on bimoraic words; generally at least one H per phonological word; some verb roots not specified for tone).
625.srule: Silva 2012: the heads of the iambic (bimoraic, right-headed) feet that follow the primary-stress foot in the left-to-right parse carry secondary stress, i.e. every second mora after the primary: (di.ˈta)(ru.ˌge), (ga.ˈki)(po.ˌa)(da.ˌri), (õʔ.ˈma)(ˌma); a single leftover final mora is usually unstressed ((yʉ.ˈkʉ)(dʉ.ˌpʉ)ri), rarely a degenerate foot ((ku.ˈye)(ˌri)). Miller 1999 gives no placement (StressTyp2 digest: 'Stems can have primary, secondary or no stress').

625.exq_: Silva 2012:69 'Stress placement in Desano generally follows a straightforward rule: stress falls on the syllable containing the last mora of a noun root morphemes. ... Thus, stress consists of left-to-right exhaustive parsing, and although degenerate feet may be allowed, it is not very common.' p.6…
625.tone: Silva 2012 sect. 2.3.2.4 (preliminary sketch): 'Desano has both stress accent and tone. There are two tones, H and L. In general, every word carries an H tone, though there are exceptions.' Lexical tone by minimal pairs (wáĩ 'name' vs wãĩ́ 'uncle', táá 'grass' vs taá 'to cut'); four surface melodies H, HL, LH, L on bimoraic words; tone independent of the duration-cued iambic stress. Miller 1999 (p.15 via StressTyp2; Silva fn.49) instead treats high pitch as the correlate of phonemic stress and 'does not distinguish stress from tone'.

tn.quote: Desano has both stress accent and tone. There are two tones, H and L. In general, every word carries an H tone, though there are exceptions. The tonal minimal pairs in (45)-(48) evidence the existence of lexical tone. These words result in four surface tone melodies: high (H), high-low (HL), low-high (LH) and low (L) in words with bimoraic structure. ... Desano exhibits a two-level tone system. Desano verbal and nominal roots may exhibit either HH, HL, or LL tone patterns, and a number of verbal affixes bear lexical high tone.
tn.cite: Silva, Wilson de Lima. 2012. A Descriptive Grammar of Desano. PhD dissertation, University of Utah.
tn.locator: sect. 2.3.2.4 'Desano Tone' p.72; sect. 1.4 'Typological Profile of Desano' pp.6-7
tn.note: Author calls the tone analysis a preliminary sketch of a 'mixed stress-tone' system: lexical H vs L tone beside predictable duration-cued iambic stress; tone left unmarked in most transcriptions.

625.cfw: Miller (1976, 1999) reports a phonemic Desano 'stress' that coincides with high tone and moves between syllables in minimal pairs, whereas Silva (2012), using vowel-duration measurements and speaker judgments, separates the two and finds stress fixed on the last mora of the root with an independent lexical high tone, an analysis that accounts for Miller's pairs and has not been contested.

morph.rootq: "The general stress pattern in SCLs is commonly observed in AALs (Dixon, 2002a:557). Stress falls on the first syllable in disyllabic words and no example is found in the source material that shows stress on the final syllable in a disyllabic word. ... In words with three syllables or more, primary stress falls on the first or second syllable. Where stress is marked on a second syllable in a polysyllabic word, a long vowel in that stressed syllable is in some cases indicated." (Besold 2012, A.3.5.1, pp.113-114). The statement is framed in terms of word syllables, not root/stem or affixes; the examples cited (mabara, bagaranj, budjan, bugaali, burnaaga, gabaanu, djarambaadhi) are unaffixed…
morph.elicq: "Information on stress assignment is found in the transcriptions of some of the early collectors. Mathews and Howitt marked many words in their wordlists for stress with an apostrophe at the end of the stressed syllable, i.e. mabara 'eye' shows the stress assigned on the first syllable in <mab'-o-ra> (U-M.1.1) and <ma'bra> (DJ-AH.1.3). Later, and in contrast, Tindale marked stress at the beginning of a stressed syllable as in the same word <'mabara> (WL-T.75)." (A.3.5, p.112). Supplemented by impressionistic remarks on present-day community pronunciation: "whereas some speakers in communities pronounce both words with a long vowel and stress on the second/final syllable" (p.113). No frame…
morph.stmt: Exclusively suffixing: "The noun structure in all SCLs is Root-(derivation)-(inflections)" (A.4, p.156); "Verbs and nouns are distinguished by the type of suffixing they can take" (A.6.1, p.284); bound pronouns: "Subject and object are marked in that order in verb-final position" (A.5.1, p.231); the only clitics described are post-inflectional enclitics (=way, =marra; A.6.9). No prefixes or proclitics are described anywhere for Dhurga; the sole non-suffixal device is a stem-final vowel alternation (a -> u) accompanying future/imperative/hortative suffixes.

627.dq: The most prominent syllable in a lexical word receives primary stress. ... at least in a large majority of cases, the placement of primary stress in monomorphemic words is restricted to one of the last three syllables of a word (Taalportaal, Primary stress in simplex words).

627.heavy: Heavy = closed syllable with a lax (B-class) vowel (VC); open syllables with tense/A-class ('long') vowels pattern as LIGHT; superheavy = A-class vowel or diphthong + C, or B-class vowel + CC (word-final only); final diphthongs attract stress; schwa syllables weightless and unstressable. Taalportaal weight scale I (after van der Hulst 1984): 'Schwa << A-class vowel / Diphthong << B-class vowel + consonant << B-class vowel + two consonants << A-class vowel / Diphthong + consonant' (scale II: 'Schwa (V) << VV << VC << VCC << VVC'). van Oostendorp 2012:354 (sec. 5 'Discussion: Is Dutch Stress Sensitive to Quantity?'): 'a four-way scale of weight for Dutch syllables: C(C) < CV(V) < CVC < CVVC, CVCC' (lowest grade = schwa syllable per the next sentence 'schwa syllables are really weaker'; the PDF renders the grade as 'C(C)'), with the comment that the evidence is 'rather strong' for the schwa and superheavy ends of the scale but 'much weaker' for the core heavy/light distinction.
627.dflt: penultimate (final open syllable -> penult; overall strongest preference is penult stress)
627.prule: Word-level main stress on one of the last three syllables (three-syllable window). Default/most frequent: penult. Antepenult is excluded when the penult is closed with a full vowel (agenda-type); word-final superheavy syllables (VVC, VCC) and final diphthongs take final stress; words ending in a plain closed VC syllable tend to antepenult stress (albatros, carnaval; weak, French loans final); final open A-vowel words tend to penult; schwa never stressed and stress falls immediately before a schwa syllable. All stated as tendencies; residue is lexically marked (kanon vs canon).
627.srule: Simplex words with full vowels (Taalportaal, Köhnlein 2015): the first stressable (non-schwa) syllable carries secondary stress unless primary stress is on the second syllable; otherwise every other syllable is stressed, clash excluded, the initial stress being kept even across a two-syllable lapse (ˌfo.no.lo.ˈɣi, ˌa.bra.ka.ˈda.bra; ˌσσˌσσˈσ in five-syllable final-stress words); words of 4+ syllables always have a secondary stress, σˈσσ has none; under antepenultimate primary stress the final syllable carries secondary stress (ˈpla.ti.ˌna, ta.ˈrɑn.ty.ˌla; debated); six-syllable final-stress words vary (medial secondary on 3rd or 4th). Whether secondary stress is quantity-sensitive is 'under debate, yet possible evidence in favour of quantity-sensitivity seems scarce'.

morph.rootq: Taalportaal 'Stress in complex words' (Köhnlein 2015): "The stress patterns in complex words (compounds, affixed words) differ from those in simplex, underived words. That is, many of the generalizations on stress placement apply to individual constituents of words (e.g. the stem) but not to the complex word as a whole ... some affixes do not affect the stress pattern of their base word at all, others attract it." 'Stress-neutral suffixes': "Most native suffixes of Dutch are stress-neutral, i.e. they do not influence the position of the main stress of their base word ... the addition of the cohering suffixes does not influence stress placement at all." morph.stmt: Taalportaal: "Dutch verbal inflection is stem-based, mostly suffixal, with a lot of syncretism" (Verbal inflection); "The plural is expressed by suffixation and/or stem alternation" (Number); in derivation "Dutch makes use of both prefixation and suffixation (but not of infixation). Moreover, Dutch has one circumfix... ge...te" and "There is a tendency for prefixation to be category-neutral (there are four exceptions: be-, ver-, ont- and ge-), whereas suffixation is often category-changing" (Derivation) — i.e. inflection is suffixal apart from the participial prefix ge- (ge-werk-t), and the derivational inventory is predominantly suffixal with a small set of unstressed verbalising prefixes.

evidence_works.detail: The article is a theoretical (OT) proposal whose Dutch case study restates Kager 1989 and Booij 1995: Dutch feet are trochaic, and optional 'semi-informal' reduction to schwa hits only the unstressed syllable directly after a stressed one (foot-internal), with reduction of all unstressed vowels as a second option, exceptions for /a, e/, and no reduction ever in absolute word-final position. Its four perception experiments (forced-choice source-word identification of excised syllables at 86.2% correct, repetition-priming lexical decision, word spotting, cross-modal priming) show that Dutch listeners use the stress cues in a syllable to tell the two members of a stress pair apart and to rule out competitor words; n

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: Three forced-choice experiments with Dutch listeners showed that the speaking rate of a preceding sentence shifts how syllable duration is heard as a cue to lexical stress: after a fast context the initial syllable of 'ali'/'kavi' fragments sounded long and stressed (more Alibi/CAvia responses), and rate also disambiguated an ambiguous second syllable. Initial-syllable duration counted far more than second-syllable duration, and for the CAvia/kaviAAR pair listeners took any long syllable in the fragment as initial stress, only two short syllables pointing to stress on the third syllable.

evidence_works.independence: not assessed (journal search; a single reading)
evidence_works.detail: Full text read. The paper states that Dutch phonological stress rules and the acoustic realisation of stress are virtually identical to English (citing Sluijter & van Heuven 1996 and Trommelen & Zonneveld 1999) but that vowel reduction is far less widespread, so unstressed full vowels are common (CELEX: 55.66% of vowel occurrences without primary stress), and Dutch listeners show a significantly smaller perceptual stress effect than English listeners; Dutch schwa has no stressed counterpart (p. 84). Praat F1/F2 measurements show the Dutch unstressed vowels shift about as much as the English on

st.weight_quote: the Dutch data suggest that closed syllables (with B-class vowels) in the penult attract stress, whereas open syllables (with A-class vowels) do not. Thus, if we regard A-class vowels as long, this implies that VC-syllables are heavy, whereas VV-syllables are light. ... diphthongs, which are strong attractors of main stress, are placed alongside with long vowels (which are not stress attracting).

tn.quote: Dutch is a language with word stress. That is, one of the syllables of a word is perceived as the prominent one, the main stress of the word. … The phoneticians Cohen, ’t Hart, and Collier have shown that main stress is realized as a pitch movement on the relevant syllable, if the word in question bears a sentence accent. … a syllable with main stress is a potential locus of sentence accent. … The accents are realized as pitch accents that consist of movements with respect to the low and the high declination line for F0 … This does not mean that stress is to be equated with pitch movement.
tn.cite: Booij, Geert (1995). The Phonology of Dutch. (The Phonology of the World's Languages.) Oxford: Clarendon Press.
tn.note: No lexical tone described: Dutch is a word-stress language; pitch movements realise sentence accent on the main-stressed syllable and are analysed as intonational tones (H*L, L*H, H*LH). Checked against the source (tone consistency check, 2026-09-23): interaction with stress tone predictable from stress -> unstated (pp. 96-97, ch. 5 'Word stress', 5.1 Introduction).

corr.words: Dutch is a language with word stress. ... main stress is realized as a pitch movement on the relevant syllable, if the word in question bears a sentence accent. ... This does not mean that stress is to be equated with pitch movement. ... Moreover, a pitch accent can also be placed on a syllable without lexical stress, for instance for metalinguistic reasons

628.dq: Vaysman 2009:62: 'In the dialect of Eastern (Meadow) Mari that I am investigating in this chapter, there is only one stress per word. The correlates of stress are fundamental frequency, amplitude, and especially duration.' (S&I 1961:9 separately attribute the choice between the two variants 'in the flow of speech' to 'overriding patterns of intonation, rhythm, and the like'.)
628.dloc: Sebeok & Ingemann 1961 p.9 ('Stress' paragraph of the Phonology chapter); Vaysman 2009 pp.62-65 (sec. 2.3.1) and p.73 (summary (53))
628.heavy: A 'full' vowel /i, e, a, ö, ü, o, u/ as opposed to the reduced vowel /ə/ (and, in Sebeok & Ingemann, harmonic final e/ö/o after a full vowel pattern with ə); Vaysman 2009:65 fn.23: 'the difference here is not between heavy and light syllables, or long and short vowels, but rather between short full and short reduced vowels'. No role for codas or vowel length.
628.dflt: initial (first vowel) — S&I 1961:9 'if none of these occurs within the word, on the first vowel'; Vaysman 2009:64 'the stress is placed on the leftmost syllable'
628.prule: Stress the rightmost (last) full vowel of the word; if the word contains only reduced vowels, stress the first vowel (Kangasmaa-Minn 1998:224 as carried by StressTyp2; Vaysman 2009 (53a) for underived words, counting UNDERLYING vowel quality). Sebeok & Ingemann 1961:9 describe the same 'nearest preceding full vowel, else first vowel' placement but in free variation with stress on the final vowel, the choice depending on intonation and rhythm; words without a harmonic/reduced final vowel are always stressed on the last vowel.
628.srule: None: 'there is only one stress per word' (Vaysman 2009:62); the binary feet diagnosed from schwa vocalization carry no additional stress ('there might be no stressed syllable in a foot', p.87). Not mentioned in Sebeok & Ingemann 1961:9 or Riese, Bradley & Yefremova 2022:28-30.

629.dq: As in English, a word never has more than one primary, or heavy, stress; and long vowels never occur unstressed.
629.heavy: Final syllable attracts stress only if CVCC or CVV(C) (superheavy / long-vowelled; final CVC does not); long vowels are always stressed; antepenult stress arises only when the last three syllables are all CV (i.e. a closed CVC or long penult/antepenult in that span keeps stress on the penult). Syllable inventory CV, CVC, CVV, CVVC#, CVCC#; 'Syllables with the structure /CVCC#/ occur only stressed.'
629.dflt: penult in LL disyllables (kátab) and after a heavy antepenult (madrása, mudarrísa); antepenult when the last three syllables are all light (kátaba, ?álamak)
629.prule: General rule: penultimate. (a) Final syllable if CVCC or CVV(C). (b) Antepenult if the last three syllables are CVCVCV(C) (all light), except 3fs perfect verb + V(C) object suffix, which keeps penult stress (ḍaṛabítu). One primary stress per word; long vowels never unstressed (two long vowels -> first shortens, stress on second).
629.srule: Not mentioned in Abdel-Massih 1975, sec. 7.5 'Stress', pp. 25-26 (the source says only 'a word never has more than one primary, or heavy, stress'). Disputed in later work: Welden 1980 (SLS 10(2), sect. 4.2, pp. 110-115), from an informant word-list test, reports pretonic secondary (rhythmic) stresses -- secondary on the first of two pretonic syllables (sànatéen), S̀ L S X́ vs S H̀ S X́ with three (màkatabúuš, mistàʕmilíin), S̀ S S̀ S X́ with four (màkatàbuháaš): trochaic pairs counted leftward from the primary, no adjacent stresses, weight deciding odd spans; Watson 2002 (ch. 5, pp. 79, 121) and Watson 2011: 'In Cairene, secondary stress is not perceived'; Aquil 2014 (PAL XXVI, not opened) argues it exists but rejects Welden's data.
629.quote: In EA stress is not a major problem, as its occurrence is almost totally predictable in terms of syllable structure. As in English, a word never has more than one primary, or heavy, stress; and long vowels never occur unstressed. Remember that EA does not permit more than one long vowel in a word; in case of two long vowels (resulting from morphological suffixation), the first gets shortened and the stress shifts to the second long vowel ... Bearing the above in mind, we can state the rules for EA stress as follows: GENERAL RULE: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable; e.g. /katab/ 'he wrot…
629.idn: 'Egyptian Arabic (EA)' = 'Arabic as spoken by the educated natives of Cairo in their daily life in informal situations' (a named variety of the language)
629.exq_: However, stress is on the penultimate syllable when (CV)CVCVCV(C) is a feminine singular past verb with a V(C) suffix: ramítu She threw it (m). šalítu She carried it (m). ḍaṛabítu She hit him. ḍaṛabítak She hit you (ms). ḍaṛabítik She hit you (fs). šalítak She carried you (ms). 630.idn: Mee (also known as Ekari, Ekagi and Kapauku), Paniai dialect (a named variety of the language); data: Data from the Paniai dialect as spoken by the second author (Niko Kobepa); joint work in Berkeley during August 2011 with follow-up work in Canberra in December 2011.…
630.tone: Two-height privative H/L word-tone system (Hyman & Kobepa 2012: 131-136): every word has at least one H at the left edge; pattern A = H on the first mora only, pattern B = H on the first two moras (three when the word begins CVCVV), all later moras L; monomoraic CV words are H; no H beyond the second syllable. The A/B choice is lexical (minimal pairs égò 'shame, shy' vs égó 'tooth', íì 'yes' vs íí 'sand', dídì 'illness' vs dídí 'mouse'); verbs carry inflectional tone patterns (P2 Indef and Ant P1 assign pattern B to all verbs); 27 of 82 CVCV pattern-A nouns become H-H before L-toned enclitics; in compounds the first member sets the pattern and the second loses its tones; no tonal interaction between full words in the sentence was found. The authors weigh marked-H, marked-L, /HL/ pitch-accent and left-edge iambic-foot (/HL/ vs /H/ melody) analyses without choosing, and find no stress.

contra.head: An earlier SIL phonology of Risaralda Chamí finds no fixed stress position in non-verbs
contra.detail: Gralow 1976 (impressionistic fieldwork, no instruments; Risaralda Chamí, 1973-74, p.30) states that stress is grammatically predictable only in verbs, where its position follows the suffix (final in the -si past forms, antepenult in the -sima forms, penult in the -e imperatives): "El acento es predecible gramaticalmente en verbos: /ko'si/ 'comió' /'kosima/ 'comió' /'kose/ 'coma' / /wa'si/ 'se fue' /'wasima/ 'se fue' /'wase/ 'váyase' / /widi'si/ 'pidió' /wi'disima/ 'pidió' /'wi'dise/ 'pida'" (p.39). For everything else she reports variable placement and no fixed syllable, which conflicts with the entry's penult-default weight rule from Aguirre Licht et al. 2013 (Karmata Rua, Antioquia): "El …

dqtr.text: But the majority of words in Embera-Chamí stress the penultimate syllable; it is the syllabic pattern. The primary stress of a word keeps moving to the right by virtue of the arrangement of unstressed and inherently stressed morphemes (pp.75-76; section headed 'El acento / Beɗea aurre jĩkuabarí' [= 'The accent']).

631.dq: Pero la mayoría de palabras en embera-chamí acentúan la penúltima sílaba, es el patrón silábico. El acento primario de una palabra se va corriendo a la derecha en virtud del arreglo de morfemas inacentuados y autoacentuados (pp.75-76; section headed 'El acento / Beɗea aurre jĩkuabarí').
631.dloc: pp. 72, 75-77 ('El acento', 'La palabra fonológica y el grupo acentual'); pp. 82-84 ('Marcación de acentos (tildes)': heavy/diphthong-final always oxytone p.82; diphthong-final examples, monosyllables, compounds, accented suffixes p.83; esdrújulas p.84)
631.heavy: heavy (pesada) = complex nucleus (diphthong Vv, vV) or closed by a consonant (VC, CVC); light (liviana) = open V, CV. No phonemic vowel length (stressed vowels lengthen allophonically).
631.prule: Default paroxytone (penult). A word whose final syllable is heavy (CVC or diphthong) is always oxytone ('siempre son agudas'). Otherwise penult, unless the final syllable is an auto-accented morpheme (lexical root in a compound, or an accented grammeme such as dative -má, prohibitive -r'ã, -á, -ɗá, -barí), which then carries the accent; in general the rightmost heavy syllable or auto-accented morpheme within the final two-syllable zone bears primary stress, and stress shifts rightward as unaccented suffixes are added (w'ẽra > wẽrárã > wẽrar'ãba). A few forms with -ruru/-turu are antepenult-stressed (w'ãrruru, kórruru, máturu) and are written with a tilde.
631.srule: No secondary-stress rule given. The source marks only the 'acento primario' and implies other accented syllables in a word (auto-accented lexemes/grammemes bring their own accent; 'En fonética se marcan los acentos de la palabra, aquí se marcará sólo el acento primario'), but states no placement or realization for non-primary accents and describes no rhythmic stress; when two accented CV syllables meet, the first vowel doubles and the second carries the primary accent.
